episode_thesis: Trend following is a second-responder to prolonged dislocations whose payoff comes from changing macro regimes, not from equity crashes: geopolitical-risk spikes tend to precede inflation, hit stocks and bonds, and lift commodities, so diversified trend (with commodity sleeves) earns positive returns in the biggest geopolitical-risk months, via commodities and bonds more than equities. Portfolio construction should favour many managers, equal risk and volatility targeting over forecast-dependent optimisation, and short-term trend adds value only if it is tested out-of-sample and backed by costly execution infrastructure.

speakers.name: Marat Molyboga
speakers.role: chief risk officer and director of research, Efficient Capital Management (about $3.5bn allocated to CTAs); guest
speakers.speaker_note: Captions have no speaker labels. Attribution follows turn structure and first-person statements (Efficient, Makita collaboration, his own papers); the early-2026 market narrative in C05 is split between Kaminski (first turn) and Molyboga (second turn). Kaastrup-Larsen's comment on commodities in equity crises (C15) is a vague recollection he says he may attribute to the wrong person.

worldview_premises.premise: Investors are human and are prone to performance chasing and hindsight bias, so an allocator's edge comes from a process that records decisions, tests a thesis per manager, and admits where it has no forecasting skill (for example, picking next year's best trend manager).
worldview_premises.support: Efficient's 25-year manager-selection experience; measured effectiveness of recorded decisions

worldview_premises.premise: CTA performance has low persistence, so ranking managers on recent returns and buying the top one or two is a poor strategy; the cross-section of managers is also extremely dispersed.
worldview_premises.support: a published study of SG index constituents (colleagues Handy and Mexi); 2022 dispersion of about 80 points between best and worst manager

worldview_premises.premise: Allocator flows follow recent performance: investors pile into CTAs after crises, wait a year or two to decide, get disappointed with ordinary returns in normal times and deallocate just before the next crisis.
worldview_premises.support: observation of client behaviour over many years; current renewed interest after a strong run

worldview_premises.premise: Institutional portfolios are driven mainly by a growth factor. Tail-risk and long-volatility strategies respond first to sudden 10-15% drops, trend responds second to dislocations lasting quarters to years, and diversifiers add uncorrelated return. Judging trend on short sharp sell-offs is a category error.
worldview_premises.support: the Makita risk mitigation framework, which he adopts

worldview_premises.premise: Forecast-dependent optimisation (mean-variance) fails out of sample because the future cannot be predicted; diversification is the only free lunch, so equal risk allocation with cluster tweaks is the better basis for portfolios.
worldview_premises.support: personal experience trying to make mean-variance work; unstable weights and poor out-of-sample results (no data shown)

worldview_premises.premise: Backtests are cheap, and reputation at stake is the discipline that limits overfitting: a bank offering hundreds or thousands of strategies bears no cost for failures, an asset manager signing off one strategy does.
worldview_premises.support: four years developing short-term strategies and learning about in-sample versus out-of-sample failure

worldview_premises.premise: Inflation regimes break the 60/40 assumptions drawn from 30-40 years of data. In high-inflation history stocks and bonds were mixed, while commodities and trend following stood out.
worldview_premises.support: his own earlier study around 2022 of high-inflation episodes

worldview_premises.premise: Managers that differ most from long-term trend (short-term, diversifying) are harder to find and die more often, even though portfolios benefit when they are included.
worldview_premises.support: Efficient's own mortality studies

decision_process.practice: A tested investment thesis for every manager, recorded decisions with measured effectiveness, and data on where the allocator has an edge.

decision_process.practice: Classify CTAs into long-term trend, short-term and diversifying groups, because they perform differently by environment.

decision_process.practice: Hold six to ten trend managers rather than one or two, with equal risk allocation, diversified across managers and time frames, via managed accounts.

decision_process.practice: Equal risk allocation with top-down tweaks for clusters of strategies, then volatility targeting at portfolio level; no mean-variance optimisation.

decision_process.practice: Combine first responders (tail risk/long vol), second responders (trend) and diversifiers according to the Makita framework, and hold trend for prolonged dislocations only.

worldview_premises.premise: History rhymes rather than repeats, so a data study of past episodes is a roadmap for the next three to five years.

worldview_premises.premise: Reactivity helps in some crises, such as fast ones like COVID, so a toolkit of different speeds is valuable on average; 'short-term' trend is broadly defined and costs rise with speed.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Guest and co-host agree on the inflation channel, but it is not tested as a mediator: the GPR-to-inflation study (long history) and the sorted-month trend result are separate and the link between them is argued, not shown.

The geopolitical sample starts in 2000 (the SG Trend index), so only about 25 years and a few extreme months support the dollar, energy and equity direction results; Kaminski herself says the dollar and energy patterns might differ over longer periods.

Molyboga's anti-overfitting argument rests on reputation risk, not evidence; the host notes the same backtest critique applies to multi-manager portfolios, and no out-of-sample record of Efficient's approach is given.

The short-term trend finding is presented from a published paper, but it is sensitive to costs and the guest concedes short-term managers use pattern recognition and decaying signals, so manager results are not a clean test of short-term trend.
Caption error: the transcript's early-June summary said CTA indices were up while equities were flat, but the text gives MSCI World and S&P 500 down 34bp; applied via the ledger correction.
The host's claim that short lookback trend models lose money comes from internal research with no numbers or cost assumptions.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Inputs the speakers treat as leading prices: the geopolitical risk index and its jumps (inflation 2-3 years later, commodities and bonds now); oil and energy prices passing through to inflation; the Fed path (cuts versus hikes) for bond trends; stock-bond and energy-equity correlations; the trend barometer for the CTA environment; allocator flows after strong CTA performance as a late-cycle sign; buyback net issuance and index concentration for equities. Horizons are one month for the GPR result, quarters to years for trend as a second responder, and three to five years for Kaminski's regime view.
reader_inferences: Molyboga and Kaminski both rely on the inflation channel but the evidence is sorted-month returns, not a mediation test, so the explanation is plausible rather than demonstrated.
Molyboga's call that trend only helps in prolonged dislocations is consistent with the geopolitical result only if the sample months are the start of persistent moves; that is not shown.

The three-way split of CTAs into long-term, short-term and diversifying and the finding that short-term lagged in 2025 but did well in 2026 suggests short-term results are regime dependent, in line with Kaastrup-Larsen's V-shaped crisis argument.
Allocator flows chasing recent CTA performance (Molyboga) and the recent strong run imply future inflows rather than a signal about returns; not a trading input for the CTAs themselves.
